query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In NiFeCoCr‐based high-entropy alloys, a controlled minor addition of an FCC metal (e.g., ~3 at% Pd) followed by an optimized annealing treatment homogenizes the distribution of magnetic exchange interactions. This more uniform exchange energy landscape reduces local anisotropy variations and domain wall pinning, thus enabling a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied magnetic fields while preserving rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-rolled or as-cast NiFeCoCr-based high‐entropy alloy with an intrinsically heterogeneous microstructure and a broad distribution of exchange energies that results in relatively moderate magnetocaloric effects and higher hysteresis.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a low atomic percentage (~3 at%) of Pd into the NiFeCoCr alloy and subject the alloy to a controlled annealing heat treatment aimed at homogenizing the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under low applied magnetic fields (e.g., up to 1 T) and across a temperature range relevant to refrigeration (roughly 100 K to above room temperature). The study should monitor magnetic entropy change, hysteresis characteristics, and mechanical properties.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in compositional and microstructural inhomogeneities that narrows the distribution in local magnetic exchange interactions and anisotropy, as evidenced by more uniform phase and grain structures.
generation.mechanism: The Pd additive, even in low concentrations, along with annealing, promotes phase homogenization by reducing local defects and compositional fluctuations. This leads to a minimized spread in exchange energy values across the material, thereby lowering domain wall pinning and hysteresis losses while maintaining efficient heat transfer and mechanical robustness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline alloy, the Pd-added and annealed sample will exhibit an enhanced magnetic entropy change (with a refrigerant capacity improvement on the order of ~25–40%), lower hysteresis losses during magnetic field cycling, and maintained or improved mechanical strength and thermal response.
generation.baseline: A NiFeCoCr-based high-entropy alloy prepared without the minor Pd addition and without the subsequent homogenizing heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for NiFeCoCr-based alloys (and similar rare-earth-free HEA systems) when minor FCC metal additives are used under annealing conditions that yield a homogenized microstructure. The behavior should be observable in low-to-moderate magnetic fields (up to ~1 T) and in the temperature range appropriate for refrigeration applications (approximately 100 K to >300 K).
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which the homogenization of exchange interactions improves the magnetocaloric response may depend sensitively on the precise composition, annealing temperature, and time. Quantitative improvements in refrigerant capacity and hysteresis reduction may vary and need further systematic study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of NiFeCoCr-based high-entropy alloy samples: one group with ~3 at% Pd addition followed by the specified annealing treatment, and a control group without Pd addition and without annealing. Characterize both groups using magnetic measurements (e.g., ΔS(T) curves, hysteresis loops) under applied magnetic fields up to 1 T and across the temperature range of 100–350 K. Complement magnetic testing with microstructural analyses (e.g., XRD, TEM, EBSD) and mechanical testing (e.g., tensile strength, ductility).
measurements: Relative cooling power (RCP) and hysteresis loop area
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Pd-added and annealed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in magnetic entropy change (and corresponding refrigerant capacity) along with reduced hysteresis—compared to the control samples—or if the microstructural analysis shows no appreciable homogenization, then the hypothesis that a reduced distribution of exchange energies governs the improved magnetocaloric response would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. RC in general is the figure of merit used to compare MCE materials giving the total heat transfer of the material over a typical refrigeration cycle. RC for a given ΔH is calculated as the integral of −ΔS(T) over a temperature range of interest: Here, TR1 and TR2 are traditionally taken to be the temperatures corresponding to the FWHM of the −ΔS(T) feature on the low and high temperature sides of the peak, respectively. We do not consider hysteretic losses here, as the M(H) loops showed negligible hysteresis, though that can be important in many systems. Figure 5 shows RC as a function of ΔH for both the annealed and as-rolled samples. The RC of 36 J/kg for a 1 T field change puts these HEAs below many other materials designed to operate in the 100–200 K range, though several factors related to pragmatic engineering issues (e.g., ductility, corrosion resistance, high thermal conductivity) may make up for this.
